authorization: User requested all 22 whole practice questions from Expand and Factorise Monic Quadratics; teaching content excluded.
method: Ordinary promotion in isolated staging, verified once and published through a checked transaction.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand binomial products and collect like terms; the hardest parts also require distributing an outside negative multiplier through the resulting trinomial.

questions.mappingNote: Source page 4 directly assesses binomial expansion using the supplied distributive method; the alignment change introduces no additional assessed skill.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The source Foundation exercise directly applies binomial expansion, including numerical multipliers.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand two products and compare their coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: The expansions are x²+7x+10 and x²−7x+10. Both answers correctly identify the common leading and constant terms and the opposite signs of the linear coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand two products and compare their coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer missing factors and terms from partially completed expansions.

questions.mappingNote: All givens and missing terms match the source tasks. Independently derived answers, in blank order: a 3; b 2; c 6, 6; d 2, 18; e 2, 6; f 3, 15; g 2x, 5x, 3; h 3x, 15x, 4; i 7x, 3, 17x; j 3x, 4, 11x. Every worked expansion is correct and follows the taught method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer missing factors and terms from partially completed expansions.

classification.difficultyReason: Model increased dimensions with binomials, expand the area and evaluate the increase.

questions.mappingNote: The new dimensions are x+4 and x+5 metres, giving x²+9x+20 square metres. At x=3, the area is 56 m² and the increase is 36 m². Prompts, units, answers and methods are correct.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model increased dimensions with binomials, expand the area and evaluate the increase.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the picture dimensions by subtracting the border on both sides, then expand their product.

questions.mappingNote: Outer area is 2x² cm². Subtracting two 5 cm borders from each dimension gives picture area (2x−10)(x−10)=2x²−30x+100 cm². Prompt, diagram, answers and skill mapping agree with the source.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the picture dimensions by subtracting the border on both sides, then expand their product.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive both pool dimensions from the outside dimensions and path width, expand the product, and evaluate it.

questions.mappingNote: Pool dimensions are 15−2x and 10−2x metres, giving 4x²−50x+150 m² and 66 m² when x=2. Both worked solutions are correct and use the taught method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive both pool dimensions from the outside dimensions and path width, expand the product, and evaluate it.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer both picture dimensions from centred frames, then expand their product.

questions.mappingNote: Centred frames give picture dimensions x−6 by x−6 in part a and x−10 by x+20 in part b. Expansions are x²−12x+36 and x²+10x−200 cm². Source givens, equality marks, solutions and mapping are correct.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer both picture dimensions from centred frames, then expand their product.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand binomial products, then combine like terms across sums, differences and a squared binomial.

questions.mappingNote: All eight prompts match the source. Independent expansion gives, in order: x²+8x+8; 5x²−5x+2; 2x²+20x+44; 2y²−y−43; 2x²+10x; −24a−45; −8x+14; −4x²+36x−78. Every worked solution correctly distributes products and subtraction signs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand binomial products, then combine like terms across sums, differences and a squared binomial.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the supplied general identity, then reverse its sum-and-product relationships to select signed integer pairs satisfying both coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: The source combines proving the binomial identity with finding factor pairs from sum-and-product conditions; the accepted expansion primary and monic-factorisation secondary mappings remain applicable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a general expansion and use coefficient relationships to identify two constants.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply distribution to binomial–trinomial products; the three-factor expression requires choosing a pair to expand first and then expanding and simplifying the intermediate product.

questions.mappingNote: All seven expressions match the source. Independently derived all cubic expansions, including cancellation of the quadratic terms in part c. Worked answers correctly extend the taught distributive method; expansion is the closest supplied skill.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extends distribution to binomial–trinomial products and a product of three binomials.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand and compare coefficients across equivalent expressions, then recognise that the final three unknowns have only two constraints and describe a family of possible values rather than a unique solution.

questions.mappingNote: The source remains an expansion exercise involving equivalent binomial expressions. The arrangement changes do not alter the accepted skill mapping or introduce another assessed task.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand equivalent expressions, compare coefficients and recognise that three letters are not uniquely determined.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the inner side as b−a, translate the guided geometric decomposition into area expressions, and equate the simplified total with c² to identify Pythagoras’ theorem.

questions.mappingNote: Stem, diagram relationships and all six parts match the source. Triangle area ab/2 and inner-square area (b-a)^2 combine to a^2+b^2=c^2. Worked expansion follows the teaching; the expansion skill is appropriate to this contextual proof.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand a squared binomial and combine geometric areas to derive Pythagoras’ theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the completed table row to expand each given binomial product, record its signed constants, and calculate their sum and product using the taught relationship.

questions.mappingNote: The source directly assesses expansion of given binomial products and sums/products of their signed constants. Factorising a quadratic is not required, so factorise-monic-quadratic is not a directly assessed secondary skill.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete expansions and identify the sum and product of the two constants using a supplied demonstration.

classification.difficultyReason: Find small integer pairs satisfying the supplied sum and product, choosing signs consistently. The labelled columns and completed example scaffold direct application of the taught relationship.

questions.mappingNote: The source and supplied teaching use signed integer pairs with specified sums and products to prepare for monic quadratic factorisation. factorise-monic-quadratic remains the closest supplied skill; no additional supplied skill is directly assessed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find signed integer pairs with specified sums and products, preparing for monic quadratic factorisation.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied PSF steps to identify signed factor pairs and write binomial factors. The hardest parts require recognising coefficients in reordered expressions, including an implicit coefficient of 1.

questions.mappingNote: Source question 3 directly assesses monic quadratic factorisation using product and sum; no secondary skill is separately assessed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Scaffolded integer factorisation using product, sum and factors, including negative constants and reordered terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer one missing constant from the given partner and the sum or product, accounting for a minus sign already printed before the blank. Both the factor structure and one constant are supplied.

questions.mappingNote: All six equations match the source. Missing numbers are respectively 3, 3, 3, 8, 1 and 2. Worked answers correctly distinguish the unsigned missing number from the signed binomial constant and verify both sum and product. Skill mappings are appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete one missing constant in supplied binomial factors using their sum and product.

classification.difficultyReason: Match six monic quadratics to shared binomial options using their sums and products.

questions.mappingNote: All six expressions and shared options match the source. Independently expanding the options confirms 1E, 2C, 3F, 4B, 5A and 6D. Cloze, short and worked answers agree; the worked explanations correctly use signed sums and products. The factorise-monic-quadratic mapping is appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match six monic quadratics to shared binomial options using their sums and products.

classification.difficultyReason: Select signed factor pairs using product and sum, including repeated factors and expressions written out of descending-power order.

questions.mappingNote: All fourteen expressions, including the original term order in k–n, match the source. Every short factorisation and worked PSF calculation is correct, including the repeated factor in c. Reordering k–n before identifying product and sum preserves each expression and supports the taught method. The factorise-monic-quadratic mapping is appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select signed factor pairs using product and sum, including repeated factors and expressions written out of descending-power order.

classification.difficultyReason: Mentally select signed factor pairs, including repeated factors and larger constants.

questions.mappingNote: All 18 expressions match the source. Every factor pair has the required sum and product, including both repeated-factor cases. The corrected source answer for part (i) is mathematically sound. Worked answers use the taught mental sum/product method; the mapping is appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Mentally select signed factor pairs, including repeated factors and larger constants.

classification.difficultyReason: Link common-factor extraction with monic quadratic factorisation. The hardest parts require extracting a negative factor, reversing the inner signs correctly, and selecting signed constants; the instruction and first-part scaffold identify the procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Source question 8 assesses monic quadratic factorisation after common-factor extraction. The supplied common-factor skill includes negative coefficients and covers the directly assessed secondary technique; factorise-negative-common-factor is absent from the supplied skill list.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The source labels this exercise Mastery; students first extract a positive or negative common factor, then factorise a monic quadratic.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied substitution to turn a quadratic with leading coefficient 25 into a monic quadratic, factorise, and substitute back.

questions.mappingNote: The expression and substitution hint match the source. With a=5x, the expression becomes a²+14a+48=(a+6)(a+8), giving (5x+6)(5x+8). Both answers and the monic-factorisation mapping are appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied substitution to turn a quadratic with leading coefficient 25 into a monic quadratic, factorise, and substitute back.

classification.difficultyReason: Form an area expression from a rectangular backyard, subtract three paved areas, and factorise the resulting monic quadratic.
